title: "Publish on GitHub or GitLab Pages"

::: {.objectives}
**In this chapter**

- Explain what publishing means here, and what only has to be done once
- Prepare the project for publishing
- Put the course online and update it later
- Check the published course, and fix what went wrong
- Know what "public" means before you press the button
:::

## What publishing means

When you press **Render Website**, RStudio builds the course into a folder called
`docs`. That folder is a complete website. Publishing means *copying that folder to
a place on the internet that shows it as a web page*.

GitHub and GitLab are websites where projects are stored online. Both can also show
the website files they hold to the public: this feature is called **Pages**, and the
result is an ordinary web address. Your course is a set of files; the platform hands
them to whoever asks.

Three words you will meet:

- **Repository**: your project folder, stored online together with its history.
- **Commit**: saving a labelled snapshot of your changes. You give it a short
  message, such as "Update chapter 3".
- **Push**: sending your saved snapshots from your computer to the online repository.

::: {.keypoint}
**Key point**

The routine every time is three steps: **render, commit, push.** The rest of this
chapter is a one-off setup, and it is fine, even normal, to have someone from your
team do that part with you.
:::

## Who does what

| | What | How often | Who |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Create the online repository, connect it to your computer, switch on Pages | Once per course | You with help, or your team |
| **B** | Render, commit, push | Every release | You |
: The one-off setup and the routine {#tbl-roles}

If your team has already set up the repository and Pages for you, skip to
[the routine](#the-routine-render-commit-push).

## GitHub or GitLab?

Your institution decides; you do not need to choose. Both do the job.

| | GitHub | GitLab |
|---|---|---|
| Address of the course | `https://<account>.github.io/<repository>/` | Depends on the installation, for example `https://<group>.pages.<institution>/<project>/` |
| Who can read it | Anyone, on the free plan | Anyone, or only members of the project, if the installation allows |
| Setup | A settings page, no extra files | Needs a small automation file; see below |
: GitHub and GitLab Pages compared {#tbl-platforms}

If your course must not be public (for example, only for enrolled students), do not
use a free public GitHub repository. Ask your team about the options on your
institution's GitLab, or about linking the course from the learning platform behind
a login.

## Before you publish

1. Finish Chapter 7: the checklist.
2. In `_quarto.yml`, set `site-url` to the address the course will have (from the
   table above). If you do not know it yet, publish once, read the address off the
   Pages settings, and then correct it.
3. Click **Render Website** one last time.

The project contains an empty file named `.nojekyll`. Leave it alone; it tells
GitHub to serve your files exactly as they are. It starts with a dot, so your
computer may hide it. That is fine.

## One-off setup

### Step A1: an online repository

::: {.panel-tabset}

## GitHub

The simplest route for a beginner is the free program **GitHub Desktop**.

1. Create an account at github.com if you do not have one. Install GitHub Desktop
   from [desktop.github.com](https://desktop.github.com) and sign in.
2. In GitHub Desktop, choose *File → Add local repository…* and pick your project
   folder. If it says that the folder is not a repository yet, click the link
   offering to create one.
3. Click **Publish repository**. Give it a name in lowercase with hyphens. For free
   Pages the repository has to be public, so **untick "Keep this code private"**.
   Click *Publish*.

## GitLab

GitLab installations differ (most institutions log in with the university account),
and there is no official desktop program. Ask your team to create the project and to
connect it to RStudio with you. Once that is done, RStudio's **Git** tab (in the
upper-right panel) does everything in the routine below.

:::

### Step A2: switch on Pages

::: {.panel-tabset}

## GitHub

1. Open the repository on github.com and click **Settings**.
2. In the left menu, click **Pages**.
3. Under *Build and deployment*, set **Source** to *Deploy from a branch*.
4. Under *Branch*, choose **main** and, in the folder drop-down next to it,
   **/docs**. Click **Save**.
5. Wait a minute or two and reload the page. The address of your course appears at
   the top.

## GitLab

GitLab shows Pages through a small automation file in the project, called
`.gitlab-ci.yml`. It differs between installations, so the template does not
include one. Ask whoever administers your GitLab; they will know the standard one
for your institution and can add it in a few minutes. Afterwards you never touch it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For the person who sets it up

A minimal file that publishes the already-built `docs` folder, as a starting
point; adapt it to your installation's runners and rules:

```yaml
pages:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - mkdir -p public
    - cp -r docs/. public/
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - public
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

It does not build the course. The author builds it in RStudio and commits the
`docs` folder.
:::

:::

## The routine: render, commit, push

Every time you want to release a new version:

1. **Render.** In RStudio, click **Render Website** and wait for it to finish
   without errors.
2. **Commit and push.** Save a snapshot and send it online. Steps below.
3. **Wait, then look.** It takes from a few seconds to a few minutes for the
   change to appear. Then open your course address and press *Ctrl+F5* so the
   browser fetches the newest version.

Committing and pushing, in detail:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## GitHub Desktop

Open GitHub Desktop. The left panel lists the changed files. There are usually
many, because the whole website is rebuilt; that is normal. In the box at the
bottom left, type a short summary such as *Update chapter 3*, and click **Commit to
main**. Then click **Push origin** at the top.

## RStudio Git tab

Open the **Git** tab. Click one file, press *Ctrl+A* to select all, and click
**Stage**. Click **Commit**, type a message, and click **Commit** again. Then click
the green **Push** arrow.

:::

## Check the published course

Open the live address and try it like a learner would:

- The navigation, sidebar and logo appear, and the colours are right.
- Pictures load, and a diagram is drawn.
- A quiz question works when you click **Check answer**.
- Search finds a word from a chapter.
- The *Slides* link in the top menu opens the slides.
- It looks right on your phone.

## When something goes wrong

| What you see | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| "404" or "Site not found" on the address | Pages is not switched on yet, or points at the wrong folder | Check Settings → Pages: branch *main*, folder */docs*. Wait a few minutes after saving |
| The page shows but with no styling, or pictures are missing | Only some files were pushed, or `.nojekyll` is missing | In GitHub Desktop check that no files are left uncommitted; check that `docs/.nojekyll` exists and re-render |
| An old version is displayed | The browser cached it, or the push did not happen | Press *Ctrl+F5*; check that GitHub Desktop says nothing is waiting to push |
| Your change is not there at all | You edited but did not render, or rendered but did not commit | Repeat render, commit, push, in that order |
| A chapter you removed still shows up | It was not cleared from `docs` | Use **Render Website** (the whole site), then commit and push again |
| A page works on the site but not in a link from your platform | The link uses the wrong address | Use the address shown in Pages settings, with `https://` |
: Publishing problems and their usual fixes {#tbl-publishing-problems}

## Fixing mistakes

Publishing is not a one-way street. If you find an error, fix the text file, render,
commit and push again; the corrected version replaces the old one. The repository
keeps every earlier version too, so a change can be rolled back with help from
someone technical.

To take the course offline, ask your team. On GitHub, making the repository private
or deleting it removes the site, and on GitLab the administrator can switch Pages
off.

## Public means public

::: {.callout-warning}
## Read this before the first push

- **Everyone can read it.** A public course is visible to the whole internet,
  including search engines.
- **Not just the finished pages: the source too.** The repository contains your
  chapter files, drafts and images, and their whole history.
- **Deleting is not enough.** If something confidential or personal is committed
  and you delete it a day later, it is still in the history. If this happens, tell
  your team at once and do not try to hide it yourself.
- **Quiz answers are readable** by anyone who looks at the page source.
  Never put an exam behind these quizzes.
- **Never commit** patient data, passwords, access tokens or unpublished results.
:::

## Your course is live

That is the whole workflow: plan on paper, write in text files, render, check,
commit, push. The first course takes the longest. The second takes a fraction of
the time, because you now know where everything is. Copy this project again for
your next one.

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz-score}
:::

::: {.question}
Which folder contains the finished website that gets published?

- [ ] `images`
- [ ] `assets`
- [x] `docs`
- [ ] `slides`

::: {.feedback}
Render Website writes the finished course into `docs`. That folder is what
GitHub Pages serves. You never edit it by hand.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
You have corrected a typo in a chapter, but the live site still shows the old text an hour later. What is the most likely reason?

- [ ] GitHub is slow today
- [x] You edited the file but did not render, commit and push
- [ ] The typo is cached in the file `.nojekyll`
- [ ] The chapter is too long

::: {.feedback}
A change only reaches the live site after all three steps. The most common cause
of "nothing happened" is one that was skipped. After a push, a few minutes' wait
and *Ctrl+F5* cover the rest.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
You accidentally committed a spreadsheet with patient names, then deleted it in the next commit. What should you do?

- [ ] Nothing; it is deleted now
- [ ] Delete the repository's Pages setting
- [x] Tell your team and your data-protection contact straight away
- [ ] Rename the spreadsheet

::: {.feedback}
The file is still in the repository's history, and if the repository is public it
may already have been seen or copied. It needs to be dealt with by people who can
remove it properly, and quickly.
:::
:::

The three steps of the routine are render, commit, and [?]{.fitb answer="push"}.
